html:
The Conoy, better known as the Piscataway, were an Algonquian people of the western shore of Chesapeake Bay, in southern Maryland along the Potomac River. They were led by a paramount chief, the tayac, who ruled several allied towns.

They farmed maize, fished and gathered oysters. When English Catholics founded Maryland in 1634, the Piscataway welcomed them, partly as allies against the Susquehannock raids from the north. The Jesuit Andrew White baptised the tayac Kittamaquund in 1640. Settlers soon pressed onto their land, and around 1700 most of the Piscataway moved north up the Susquehanna, where the English called them Conoy. They later joined the Haudenosaunee and moved on to Canada. Families who stayed in Maryland gained state recognition in 2012. See Piscataway and the neighbouring Nanticoke.
